the input layer encodes 𝑁𝑖 model parameters, which are propagated 
through hidden layers using ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation 
functions [75]. The output layer, with a linear activation function, 
results in the PCA coefficients corresponding to a given pollution field. 
For a given Neural Network architecture topology, the model is trained 
on 𝑁train RANS samples using the ADAM optimization algorithm [76], 
which iteratively updates the weights and biases to minimize the 
regression error. To avoid overfitting, the training procedure is stopped 
if no improvements are detected on validation loss on more than 10 
epochs, with the restoration of the better model weights.
Our implementation is based on the PyTorch library [77].
The MLP architecture is defined by 22 hyperparameters, listed 
in Table 2 together with their interval. These intervals delimit the 
search space for the optimization process, which is performed using 
the validation dataset, as detailed in Section 2.2.3.
2.2.2. Dense layer Convolutional Encoder–Decoder with skipped connec-
tions (DCED)
Unlike the PCA+MLP approach, which reduces the dimensionality 
of the physical pollution fields by a linear combination of principal 
components before feeding the MLP, the DCED architecture operates 
directly on high-dimensional structured data. DCED leverages a con-
volutional encoder–decoder topology to extract and reconstruct spatial 
features. The encoder compresses the input via convolution and pooling 
layers to capture hierarchical patterns, while the decoder restores 
resolution through upsampling. Skip connections link encoder and de-
coder stages at corresponding levels, potentially preserving fine-grained 
spatial details lost during downsampling. These nonlinear processes 
suggest that DCED may perform better compared to the more compact 
linear PCA + regression model pipelines.
DCED is composed of fully convolutional layers that are designed 
and optimized for tasks involving structured spatial data, typically 
requiring image-like input rather than the current vector of input 
parameters 𝜽 ∈ R𝑁𝑖 . Thus, we apply a single layer neural network to 
map the input vector to a synthetic 64 × 64 (𝑁𝑝) image. As illustrated 
in Fig. 6, this image enters the encoder–decoder, which processes it 
through its structure. The final linear layer then outputs the predicted

2.2.3. Hyperparameter optimization using non-dominated sorting genetic 
algorithm
The MLP and DCED hyperparameters defined in Tables 2 and 3 
are optimized using the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II 
(NSGA-II) [78], a widely adopted multiobjective evolutionary algo-
rithm [79,80]. Like other genetic algorithms (GAs), NSGA-II evolves a 
population of candidate solutions through iterative processes of selec-
tion, crossover, and mutation, mimicking natural selection. However, it

extends traditional GAs by incorporating a non-dominated sorting ap-
proach and an elitist strategy to handle multiple conflicting objectives 
efficiently.
This method is used to tune the training configurations for each 
network, resulting in optimized models whose hyperparameters are 
jointly adjusted to satisfy four competing objectives:
1. The regression error (𝜉) is computed as the normalized mean 
square error defined in Eq. (15). To ensure the overall predictive 
capacity in the population, a restriction on regression errors is set 
to 10%, that is, samples with a regression error above 10% will 
automatically be considered as non-dominant. This value was set 
after preliminary tests and ensures relatively high-quality networks 
while allowing exploration of the parametric space.
2. To evaluate the surrogate model’s ability to predict changes in flow 
patterns, we also consider a binary classification error rate (𝛾) 
which is defined as the proportion of misclassified samples: 
𝛾 = 𝐹 𝑁 + 𝐹 𝑃𝐹 𝑁 + 𝐹 𝑃 + 𝑇 𝑁 + 𝑇 𝑃 , (17)
where 𝐹 𝑁 (False Negatives) and 𝐹 𝑃 (False Positives) correspond 
to incorrectly classified samples, while 𝑇 𝑁 (True Negatives) and 
𝑇 𝑃 (True Positives) represent correctly classified ones. A sample 
is considered positive if a counterclockwise vortex is predicted, and
negative otherwise.
3. The training dataset size refers to the number of random sam-
ples drawn from the total 𝑁train samples available for training. 
Reducing the size of the training dataset, while preserving learning 
efficiency, is essential for lowering the substantial computational 
cost associated with generating CFD databases.
4. The size of the neural network, quantified by the number of 
trainable parameters, affects its generalization ability, computa-
tional cost, and susceptibility to overfitting. It is therefore essential 
to minimize network size while preserving sufficient capacity to 
accurately model the underlying physical phenomena.
NSGA-II identifies a diverse set of non-dominated solutions, i.e.,
those that are optimal in at least one objective given a set of all others. 
To maintain population diversity and convergence stability, NSGA-II 
employs a crowding distance mechanism and a (𝛽+𝜙) selection strategy, 
where 𝛽 represents the parent population and 𝜙 the offspring. This 
elitist approach ensures that the best solutions are preserved over gen-
erations. The resulting Pareto front provides a set of optimal trade-offs, 
allowing for informed selection of model configurations that balance 
accuracy, complexity, and data efficiency. Our NSGA-II implementation 
is based on the Pyhton library Pymoo [81].

3.1. Convergence analyses and sample classification
Before training the surrogate models, we filter out non-convergent 
samples, as these can adversely affect the training process. To assess 
convergence, we use as reference metric the mean error in the transport 
equations of momentum (Eq. (2)) and the turbulent kinetic energy 
(TKE) (Eq. (6)), normalized by their values in the first iteration. Fig. 
7 shows the percentage of data retained as a function of the selected 
thresholds. Based on this figure, we select a threshold of 0.05 for both 
relative errors to ensure high quality samples while retaining more than 
80% of the originally generated database. Then, the number of samples 
available for training, validation and testing is 𝑁samples = 𝟒𝟗𝟓𝟗𝟎.
As mentioned above, we evaluate the performance of the surrogate 
model based on the classification error rate, along with three additional 
objectives. Using the criterion defined in §2.1.1 (namely, ∫𝛺left 𝐜 𝑑𝐴 >
∫𝛺right 𝐜 𝑑𝐴 for clockwise-rotating vortices, and vice versa) we identify a 
total of 2132 converged samples that exhibit counterclockwise vortices, 
representing 4.3% of the total dataset. Fig. 8 presents the joint and

occurrence of counterclockwise vortex formation, which offers insight 
into the combinations of parameters that drive this inversion. The 
results indicate that counterclockwise vortices are more likely to occur 
under the following conditions: (i) 𝜃 ∈ (90 ◦, 135◦), where both the 
ground and the inner wall of the downwind building are heated; (ii) 
strongly heated surfaces, indicated by large temperature differences 
(𝛥𝑇 ); and (iii) low heat release from the emission source. These findings 
are consistent with previous studies linking counterclockwise vortex 
patterns with strong thermal effects [48]. Although this may seem 
counterintuitive, strong thermal effects are associated with low emis-
sion heat release, as this maximizes the temperature gradient between 
heated surfaces and the surrounding cooler air.
Furthermore, we observe a subtler correlation between counter-
clockwise vortices and certain parameters of the RANS model, partic-
ularly those influencing the velocity and turbulent kinetic energy inlet 
profiles (𝐶𝜖2, 𝜅, and 𝑝𝑘). This behavior might be associated with the 
balance between momentum turbulent diffusion and thermal effects, 
as an increase in turbulent mixing would reduce the thermal gradients. 
However, the mechanisms underlying these interactions appear to be 
more complex and require further investigation. For completeness, the 
joint and marginal distributions of the entire set of input parameters 
are provided in Appendix C.
As we will see in the next subsection, vortex inversion presents a 
key challenge to the surrogate model’s accuracy, as it reflects a highly 
nonlinear response to variations in the input parameters. Therefore, we 
deemed it important to characterize the input combinations that lead 
to this behavior, as this can help to design balanced and representative 
training datasets for future work.

parent population and an offset mechanism to promote exploration of

A comparison of the Pareto fronts obtained for the PCA+MLP and 
DCED architectures is presented in Fig. 10, which illustrates the set

objectives. As expected, the Pareto fronts confirm that improving one

performance, both DCED and PCA+MLP achieve a similar classifica-

Due to its architectural design, the DCED has a network size approx-

This increased complexity leads to significantly higher computational 
costs during training. However, PCA+MLP appears to require larger 
training datasets to achieve regression errors comparable to those of 
DCED. The opposite trend is observed for the classification error.
Analysis of the candidate architectures generated during the NSGA-
II search reveals consistent trends in network performance. For the 
PCA+MLP models, relatively shallow architectures (2–4 layers) consis-
tently outperform deeper configurations, which appear to be affected 
by vanishing gradient effects. The best-performing four-layer networks 
exhibit an increase–decrease–increase neuron pattern, suggesting the 
presence of a bottleneck that promotes compact feature extraction. 
Early stopping acted as the primary regularization mechanism, and 
additional techniques such as dropout or weight decay did not yield 
measurable improvements. For DCED models, performance was pri-
marily influenced by the number of filters in the initial convolutional 
layers, with higher entry-layer filter counts generally leading to better 
predictive accuracy. While the NSGA-II search successfully identified 
several high-performing architecture configurations, the computational 
cost of evaluating many candidate networks per generation makes this 
approach impractical for training large ensembles of surrogate models.

4. Conclusion
This study developed and evaluated non-intrusive surrogate models 
for pollution dispersion in a thermal street canyon. A comprehensive 
two-dimensional RANS database was generated, covering key physi-
cal and modeling parameters such as turbulence settings, inlet pro-
files, emissions, source height, heat release, and solar irradiance. We 
benchmarked a PCA+MLP approach against a convolution encoder–
decoder architecture, with model architectures and training hyperpa-
rameters optimized via NSGA-II to balance accuracy, complexity, and 
data efficiency. Performance was assessed using a combined regression–
classification framework capturing both field predictions and vortex 
orientation.
The analysis indicates that both surrogate approaches, PCA+MLP 
and DCED, exhibit similar performance in terms of regression and 
classification errors. The PCA+MLP approach is considerably more 
computationally efficient during training, whereas DCED demonstrates 
slightly better performance in terms of regression accuracy.
Despite the simplicity of two-dimensional street-canyon geometry, 
performance decreases when thermal effects dominate and the main 
vortex is inverted. This is mainly due to the highly nonlinear response 
to input parameters in this regime and the limited number of samples 
available to fully capture such patterns. In this context, the current 
database could be further extended by heavily sampling the thermally 
dominated regime, as described by the input parameter ranges in 
Section 3.1, which primarily correspond to strong heating of the ground 
and the inner wall of the downwind building.
Surrogate models could be further improved using more complex ar-
chitectures, such as generative adversarial neural networks (GANs) and 
physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). We make our dataset and 
surrogate modeling efforts publicly available in the hope of fostering 
the development of emulators for complex thermal flows.
This work highlights the potential and limitations of data-driven 
surrogate models as computationally efficient alternatives to traditional 
CFD simulations for urban environmental assessments. The findings 
emphasize the importance of carefully handling nonlinear regimes, par-

title: Surrogate modelling for the forecast of Seveso-type atmospheric pollutant dispersion
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a framework for the development of a computationally-efficient surrogate model for air pollution dispersion. Numerical simulation of air pollution dispersion is of fundamental importance for the mitigation of pollution in Seveso-type accidents, and, in extreme cases, for the design of evacuation scenarios for which long-range forecasting is necessary. Due to the high computational load, sophisticated simulation programs are not always useful for prompt computational studies and experimentation in real time. Surrogate models are data-driven models that mimic the behaviour of more accurate and more complex models in limited conditions. These models are computationally fast and enable efficient computer experimentation with them. We propose two methods. The first method develops a grid of independent dynamic models of the air pollution dispersion. The second method develops a reduced grid with interpolation of outputs. Both are demonstrated in an example of a realistic, controlled experiment with limited complexity based on an approximately 7 km radius around the thermal power plant in Šoštanj, Slovenia. The results show acceptable matching of behaviour between the surrogate and original model and noticeable improvement in the computational load. This makes the obtained surrogate models appropriate for further experimentation and confirms the feasibility of the proposed method.
source: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment

Abstract
This paper presents a framework for the development of a computationally-efﬁcient surrogate model for air pollution
dispersion. Numerical simulation of air pollution dispersion is of fundamental importance for the mitigation of pollution in
Seveso-type accidents, and, in extreme cases, for the design of evacuation scenarios for which long-range forecasting is
necessary. Due to the high computational load, sophisticated simulation programs are not always useful for prompt
computational studies and experimentation in real time. Surrogate models are data-driven models that mimic the behaviour
of more accurate and more complex models in limited conditions. These models are computationally fast and enable
efﬁcient computer experimentation with them. We propose two methods. The ﬁrst method develops a grid of independent
dynamic models of the air pollution dispersion. The second method develops a reduced grid with interpolation of outputs.
Both are demonstrated in an example of a realistic, controlled experiment with limited complexity based on an approx-
imately 7 km radius around the thermal power plant in S ˇ osˇtanj, Slovenia. The results show acceptable matching of
behaviour between the surrogate and original model and noticeable improvement in the computational load. This makes the
obtained surrogate models appropriate for further experimentation and conﬁrms the feasibility of the proposed method.
Keywords Air pollution /C1 Seveso-type accident /C1 Pollution dispersion /C1 Surrogate modelling /C1 Dynamic systems /C1
Data-driven modelling
1 Introduction
A framework for the development of a computationally-
efﬁcient surrogate model for air pollution dispersion is
studied in this paper.
Surrogate modelling (Keane et al. 2008; Koziel and
Leifsson 2013; Jiang et al. 2020) is an engineering method
that is used when we cannot compute the response of the
model of the system of interest easily enough. It is a
method that helps to alleviate computationally demanding
computations necessary for tasks like design optimisation,
design-space exploration, and various computationally
intensive analyses. Speeding up computations can be done
by constructing an approximation model known as a sur-
rogate model, meta model, emulation model, or emulator.
The surrogate model is usually developed by selecting a
suitable data-driven black-box model. Such a model is
obtained from the input-output response of the original
mathematical model. It is constructed based on appropri-
ately selected input values that excite the original mathe-
matical model in the region of interest as illustrated in
Fig. 1.
Surrogate models have been used in different scientiﬁc
ﬁelds for different tasks, see (Alizadeh et al. 2020) for a
review. The methodology is used also in atmospheric sci-
ences for dispersion modelling, e.g. (Carnevale et al. 2012;
Bowman and Woods 2016; Gunawardena et al. 2021;L e
et al. 2019; Francom et al. 2019; Girard et al. 2020). The
relevance of dispersion modelling is non-disputable and

addressed in numerous studies dealing with different
environments, situations and methods, e.g. (Ravina et al.
2021).
The purposes of developing surrogate models range
from uncertainty quantiﬁcation (Francom et al. 2019)t o
spatial-deposition prediction (Gunawardena et al. 2021).
The core of all applications is to replace a computationally
demanding model with a faster surrogate one. Details of
some recent investigations are as follows.
To investigate the relative impact of a collection of
uncertain model inputs and their interactions on the outputs
of the atmospheric dispersion for the Fukushima nuclear
catastrophe, Girard et al. ( 2016) applied Sobol’s global
sensitivity analysis using Gaussian-process emulation. At
64 measurement locations, the emulators’ ability to fore-
cast time- and space-aggregated gamma dose rates, as well
as time-integrated gamma radiation rates, were assessed.
Le et al. ( 2019) describe the use of surrogate models for
the prediction of integrated statistical measures, e.g. Root
Mean Square Error, based on inputs describing meteoro-
logical forecasts and a source term. The authors have
shown an application of surrogate modelling for replacing
an Eulerian model for the Fukushima event.
Pal et al. ( 2019) developed a surrogate model of phy-
sics-based radiation model using deep neural networks to
reduce the computational cost.
For 2D dose prediction in a Brazilian nuclear power
plant, Desterro et al. ( 2020) utilised a Deep Rectiﬁer
Neural Network. The method was developed for immediate
prediction up-to 1 h after the accident and considered ﬁve
model inputs (wind velocity, wind direction, position x,
position y and time after the accident started). The data
samples for the investigation were generated by the simu-
lation model and, consequently, the obtained model can be
considered as a surrogate.
Gunawardena et al. ( 2021) proposed a data-driven sur-
rogate model to predict the spatial deposition of radioactive
materials from a nuclear power plant for a single radio-
logical release over a wide area for a particular period of
48 h. A grid of linear regression and logistic models is used
for the surrogate model with categorical variables from an
NWP system as inputs.
Carnevale et al. ( 2012) used a grid of neural networks
for the static mapping between precursor emissions in each
cell and its neighbouring cells and PM10 pollutant in a
domain of interest.
Bowman and Woods ( 2016) proposed a surrogate model
of atmospheric dispersion for a Gaussian puff model. The
surrogate model is composed of basis functions whose
coefﬁcients are modelled with a Gaussian-process model.
They compare different modelling methods with the
uncertainty quantiﬁcation of coefﬁcients. The surrogate
model is a static model and does not take dynamics into
account. The static model means that the surrogate model
output at every time instant does not encounter the past or
derivations of input and/or output variables.
Uncertainty quantiﬁcation of spline coefﬁcients is also
the purpose of (Francom et al. 2019), which efﬁciently uses
Bayesian adaptive splines for surrogate modelling to which
they use categorical inputs, i.e. discrete values from a ﬁnite
set of choices from a numerical weather prediction (NWP)
system. The purpose of the developed surrogate model is
the characterisation of atmospheric release. In particular,
the authors model the weights of empirical orthogonal
functions in space and time for plume emulation using the
adaptive splines.
Mallet et al. ( 2018) built a meta-model that replicates
the key aspects of the air quality model ADMS-Urban to
simulate NO 2 and PM10 emissions on an urban scale with
street resolution and continuous emissions from emission

sources. The original model lacks a temporal dimension in
inputs and outputs and is static with low-dimensional
inputs and high-dimensional outputs. The principal com-
ponent analysis is used to condense the model’s outputs
before multiple linear regression and Kriging interpolate
them.
For anticipating atmospheric dispersion of methane
(CH4) in 2D over complicated terrain, Lauret et al. ( 2016)
developed cellular automata paired with an artiﬁcial-neu-
ral-network model. A dynamic model based on wind ﬁeld
data processed with Computational-Fluid-Dynamics simu-
lation is utilised to supply input data for the artiﬁcial neural
network.
A surrogate model for the Computational-Fluid-
Dynamics wind model is developed by Moonen and
Allegrini ( 2015). The surrogate model was a Gaussian-
process model applied in a case study representing an
urban area.
A surrogate model of a Computational-Fluid-Dynamics
model of pollution dispersion (Mendil et al. 2021) and
recently (Mendil et al. 2022) is a deep-neural-network
model that mimics the accidental release of a radioactive
pollutant from multiple sources for up to 2 h ahead in an
urban area.
There are other uses of surrogate modelling that prove
the utility of the methodology. Each of the described cases
is a bit different in the model’s purpose or different in the
methods used, but with a common goal of reducing com-
putational burden with the use of some approximation.
Nevertheless, the listed surrogate models only utilise the
information about the present and not about the past. In this
sense, they are not dynamic models. One possible reason is
that using information from previous time instants con-
siderably increases the dimension of input space.
1.1 Problem statement
The problem at stake, different from those published, deals
with modelling a dispersion of a pollutant with a single
source of pollution over complex terrain. In Europe, major
accidents involving dangerous chemicals are prevented and
controlled through the Seveso Directive (European Com-
mission 2020). Seveso-type industrial facilities and nuclear
power plants have the potential for accidents with serious
consequences, especially when the release occurs over
complex terrain. When such an accident occurs, the con-
sequences for the environment and the human population
must be quickly forecasted. Air pollution dispersion in a
complex environment is commonly modelled and simu-
lated with the Lagrangian particle dispersion model (Girard
et al. 2020), where the cost for its forecast accuracy is a
heavy computational burden. The dispersion model is a
dynamic model, which adds to its complexity.
The problem we tackle is to develop a surrogate model
that will provide reliable forecasts of air pollution disper-
sion relatively quickly so that authorities will have enough
time and information to act upon it. The surrogate model
also should take into account the dynamics of the air pol-
lution dispersion. The primary goal is to improve the
computational speed of prediction to use the model for
potential experimentation and long-range forecasting, i.e.
forecasting for an extensive period of time, as long as
information on weather variables or average weather
variables is available. If the surrogate model is available
for potentially important Seveso objects in advance, then in
the event of a disaster, emergency services could use
meteorological forecasts and calculate the dispersion
forecasts quickly. The investigation is intended for the
ground layer because that is where most people are
exposed. The investigation can be done also for higher
layers with the same methods and corresponding data. The
ground layer is usually also the most complex layer due to
the inﬂuence of terrain and land use.
1.2 Contribution
We propose two methods for modelling an input-output
dynamic surrogate model of continuous point-source
originating pollution over complex terrain based on mete-
orological variables obtained from an NWP system or other
sources of weather information.
The contribution of the investigation is as follows:
• A method for the modelling of a surrogate model of air
pollution dispersion based on meteorological variables
as inputs and 2D representation of relative pollution
concentration at the output as a grid of independent
dynamic models (GIM) for each output cell.
• A method for the modelling of a surrogate model of air
pollution dispersion based on meteorological variables
as inputs and 2D representation of relative pollution
concentration at the output as a reduced grid of dynamic
models with interpolation of outputs (RGI).
• A fast and applicable case-study demonstration of the
listed methods on a simulated Seveso-type point release
of a pollutant over complex terrain.
In addition to developing the surrogate model, the con-
tributed methods also can be used for modelling a data-
driven dispersion model if the necessary training data is
available. Nevertheless, this is not the emphasis of the
paper.
The emphasis of the paper is on developing a surrogate
model that reduces the computational burden of model
prediction and forecasting with acceptable accuracy. Note
that this paper is not about the particular data-driven
machine learning method nor is its focus exclusively on the

2 Mathematical model and numerical
simulation
The case study for demonstrating the development of a
surrogate model for pollution dispersion is the S ˇ osˇtanj
thermal power plant. The pollution dispersion of this power
plant frequently attracts attention and was also used for
early modelling with artiﬁcial neural networks (Boz ˇnar
et al. 1993).
A constant and continuous sulphur-dioxide (SO 2) pol-
lution source emission of unit value was presumed, and
which can be, when necessary, proportionally sized for
real-life situations. The location of the Sˇ osˇtanj power plant
is at the edge of the Velenje Basin in Slovenia (Fig. 2). It is
surrounded by the Alps to the north and north-west. The
basin consists of narrow valleys with rivers ﬂowing along
them and, as such, represents highly complex terrain.
Winds are stronger on elevated levels and weaker in the
basin. A temperature inversion in winter and other cir-
cumstances additionally complicate the situation.
Pollution dispersion in such a complex terrain was
successfully modelled by an air pollution Lagrangian par-
ticle dispersion model (Mlakar et al. 2015), which repre-
sents a suitable method to deal with the complexity of the
terrain. The Lagrangian particle dispersion model was
combined with a corresponding meteorological preproces-
sor able to reconstruct a three-dimensional diagnostic
nondivergent wind ﬁeld. In particular, the SPRAY
Lagrangian particle dispersion model (Castelli et al. 2018),
the MINERVE diagnostic mass consistent wind ﬁeld model
(Finardi et al. 1998) and the SURFPRO meteorological
preprocessor (Finardi et al. 1997) were used for the dis-
persion modelling (Mlakar et al. 2015). Inputs in the
Lagrangian particle dispersion model were weather vari-
ables that can be collected at different weather stations or
weather-forecast variables, the digital model of the terrain
heights, and land cover data of the region. Realistic
information regarding land use was used in the Lagrangian
particle dispersion model. The weather-forecast variables
are valuable, especially in the case of major accidents

involving dangerous chemicals, where we would like to
forecast the direction and values of pollution dispersion.
For our demonstration, we did not use all the weather
variables as described in (Mlakar et al. 2015), but have
made a study for the simpliﬁed weather situation as fol-
lows. The temperature proﬁle, wind velocity and direction
were provided only at two altitudes, 10 m and 500 m, at the
location of the thermal power plant in Sˇ osˇtanj. The weather
was presumed sunny with a clear sky. The output variable
was the relative concentration of SO 2, but any other
chemical of interest could be used in the study. The relative
concentration (s/m 3) is a ratio between absolute pollutant
concentration in lg/m3 and the rate of emission (kg/s)
(Mlakar et al. 2019). The relative concentration enables
rescaling the results to any other form of pollutant emis-
sion. The region of interest was 15 /C2 15 km described with
100 /C2 100 square cells of 150 /C2 150 m each. Conse-
quently, we dealt with the situation in 10,000 cells.
What we were striving for was the computational aspect
of the described model. Nevertheless, the matching
between the Lagrangian particle air pollution dispersion
model output and the real situation in the ﬁeld played a
noticeable role in our study, but we were aware that it can
be improved a bit further with additional training data and
modelling effort. The software was run on an i9 desktop
computer with MS Windows operating system. The model
at the designated computer calculated every half-hour
response at approximately a few tens of seconds. While this
was an expected and acceptable computational perfor-
mance, it was too slow to serve for numerical experimen-
tation, which would be necessary for the real-time
forecasting of accidents and especially not for long-range
forecast studies because the time of calculation increases
linearly with the length of the forecast horizon.
We took the developed Lagrangian particle dispersion
model combined with the corresponding meteorological
preprocessor as a benchmark and tried to improve the
computational performance at an acceptable loss of accu-
racy with a surrogate model.
3 Methods
3.1 Surrogate modelling
3.1.1 The modelling procedure
The brief procedure for developing a surrogate model in
our case is as follows (Fig. 3).
1. The development of a Lagrangian particle dispersion
model with the accuracy suitable for the model’s
purpose.
2. Dataset generation with the Lagrangian particle dis-
persion model for surrogate modelling.
3. The selection of a model-development method for the
surrogate model.
4. The selection of a surrogate-model structure (regres-
sors, regression method, etc.).
5. Data-driven modelling of a large number of indepen-
dent models, each for a cell of interest, or modelling of
a smaller number of independent models and interpo-
lation of their responses to the ﬁeld of cells.
6. The prediction of the obtained surrogate model with
data not used for modelling.
3.1.2 Constraints and assumptions
One of the most important steps in surrogate modelling is
the generation of input samples that are intelligently dis-
tributed within the entire input space. This is usually done
with optimal experimental design or with active learning
(Breiman et al. 2017). In the case of atmospheric phe-
nomena, the input variables utilised for modelling are
commonly weather variables. This was also in our case.
Values at the inputs were not obtained with a designed
experiment and its implementation, but we used weather
forecasts from a numerical weather simulator. The reason
for this choice is that realistic combinations of values of

input variables cannot ﬁll all the subspaces in the input-
variables space because all possible combinations are not
natural. Therefore, lots of combinations never occur.
Consequently, we use data from available weather sources
and not optimal experimental design or active learning.
This particular selection of input data means that the
number of data is not optimal and a large amount of data is
necessary to encompass the relevant information.
The dispersion provided by the Lagrangian particle
dispersion module has a resolution of 10,000 cells, with
each cell measuring 150 /C2 150 m. This means that we deal
with a system of 10,000 outputs, which introduces an
identiﬁcation problem with the excessive number of out-
puts. Such a problem can be tackled with dimension-re-
duction methods, e.g. (Girard et al. 2020). We decided to
approach the problem differently and offer an alternative
solution. The idea is to divide the model into a large
number of submodels, as it was utilised in (Gunawardena
et al. 2021; Carnevale et al. 2012), under the assumption
that outputs do not inﬂuence each other. Nevertheless, the
results described in the continuation showed that this
working assumption provides some applicable results.
Further research on alternative models and some output
reduction methods applicable to this problem is envisaged
for the future.
3.1.3 Performance metrics
Modelling performance was evaluated with two cost
functions. The ﬁrst is selected to evaluate time-dependent
predictions of every submodel in the entire system in
comparison with the original system. This evaluation is
done with the standardised mean-squared error—SMSE
(Le et al. 2019; Rasmussen and Williams 2006):

SMSE is a frequently used standardised measure for the

0 and 1, where the value 0 is the result of a perfect model.

The coefﬁcient of determination is deﬁned as

The value is between 0 and 1, and a bigger value is better.
The presentation of pollution dispersion at ground level
in our case is a two-dimensional ﬁeld—an image of the
dispersion. Consequently, the second selected cost func-

Therefore it does not validate concentration levels, but the

Ensembles of decision trees and a Gaussian-process grid

3.2 Decision trees
The literature provides many different algorithms for
learning decision trees, which can be classiﬁcation or
regression trees (Breiman et al. 2017). While classiﬁcation
trees have a categorical output that indicates belonging to a
ﬁnite set of outputs, regression trees provide numeric
responses. A binary model tree, whether it is of a classi-
ﬁcation or regression type, consists of a split node with a
threshold test of a particular variable xi 2 X , where X is a
set of regressors. Given identiﬁcation data
D ¼ð x; yÞj x 2 Rp; y 2 Rr , where x is the vector of
regressors (inputs) and y is the output, a model tree parti-
tions the input space Rr into several partitions, called
leaves. The split node creates a binary partition of the input
space and has left and right offspring nodes. Such tree-like
structures are frequently used for surrogate modelling
(Alizadeh et al. 2020). They are robust, have the internal
regressors’ selection mechanism, are computationally
efﬁcient, are interpretable to a certain extent, etc. The

disadvantage is that piece-wise continuous estimates, as in
the case of regression trees, may create certain inaccuracy,
particularly for small trees.
The accuracy of regression trees can be improved with
the use of tree ensembles (Mendes-Moreira et al. 2012;
Aleksovski et al. 2016). Tree ensembles are created from
several uncorrelated regression-tree models. A combina-
tion of the imperfect predictions obtained from each model
tree should improve the prediction accuracy over a single
tree and thus provide a more accurate model. Different
principles exist to create ensembles. One of them is the
bagging principle (Breiman 1996; Breiman et al. 2017). In
bagging, bootstrap replicates are created, i.e. random
samples with replacement of the training dataset D that
have an equal number of data points as the training set.
Each of the replicates Di is used to build one model tree.
The learning procedure starts by creating n bootstrap
replicates of the training data D. Using each of the n data
samples, a collection of model trees is built: m1; m2; ... ; mn.
Denoting the predictions of the n single-output model trees
of the ensemble with ^fiðxÞ, the overall prediction from the
model tree ensemble is the average of the base model
predictions for one output variable:
^yðxÞ¼ 1n Xni¼1 ^fiðxÞ: ð5Þ
The rationale for selecting ensembles of bagged regression
trees for modelling surrogate models was twofold: (1)
learning of regression trees is faster than for other tested
models and (2) ensembles improved the accuracy of pre-
dictions. Other selections might be viable as well.
3.3 Gaussian-process grid
Gaussian process modelling, also known as kriging, is a
further method used in surrogate modelling (Alizadeh et al.
2020). Gaussian process models (Rasmussen and Williams
2006; Kocijan 2016) describe the input-output mapping of
data f ðxÞ from regression vector x with a Gaussian process
(GP). GP is a stochastic process containing random vari-
ables f ðxiÞ with a normal probability distribution,
pðf ðx1Þ; ... ; f ðxN Þj x1; ... ; xN ÞÞ ¼ N ðm; KÞ: ð6Þ
The vectors xi are regressor vectors, f is the GP, m is the
mean vector and K is the covariance matrix of the Gaussian
distribution N . In GP modelling, we describe the GP with
a mean function and a covariance function,
mi ¼ mðxiÞ; Kij ¼ Cðxi; xjÞ; ð7Þ
where mðxiÞ is the mean function and Cðxi; xjÞ is the
covariance function. GP models are ﬂexible function
approximators, which can be used to represent complex
structures with covariance kernels (Kocijan 2016).
When dealing with the grid structure of output data,
grid-based covariance approximations can be utilised
(Wilson and Nickisch 2015). This is the way to decrease
computational costs in training and prediction. In the case
of multidimensional inputs on a Cartesian grid,
x 2 X 1 /C2/C1/C1/C1/C2 X p, and a product kernel across the grid
dimensions, Cðxi; xjÞ¼ Qpk¼1 Cðxik; xjkÞ, then the n /C2 n
covariance matrix K can be expressed as a Kronecker
product K ¼ K1 /C10/C1/C1/C1/C10 Kp. The product of grid sizes in
all the dimensions N ¼ Qpi¼1 np is a product of the number
of points np per grid dimension. The method takes
advantage of the computational properties of a grid-based
covariance matrix via the structured kernel interpolation.
The reader is referred to (Wilson and Nickisch 2015) for
more details.
4 Results and discussion
4.1 Grid of independent models—GIM
4.1.1 Data
Data for training, validation and testing were obtained with
the simulation of air pollution Lagrangian particle disper-
sion model for the S ˇ osˇtanj thermal power plant. The data
sequence contained three years of data (July 2018–July
2021) with a 30-min sampling time. The data sequence
contained SO 2 concentration as a system’s output signal
and 7 meteorological variables as a system’s input signals,
which were temperature, wind velocity and wind direction
at heights 10 m and 500 m, the global solar IR radiation
and the ground projection of the dispersion forecast for
each time instant.
This set of more than 52,500 data pieces was divided
into training, validation and test sets. Since we need as
much data as possible for training to get as much infor-
mation as possible, we ended dividing data into 51 subsets
where one was immediately set aside as the test dataset
(June 2021–July 2021), while the rest of the data was used
for training and validation (July 2018–May 2021). The test
data incorporated samples at the end of the completed
dataset.
The data that was not used for the test was normalised,
namely centred to have a mean of 0 and scaled to have a
standard deviation of 1. The obtained mean values and
variances were then also used for the normalisation of the
test data.

4.1.2 Structure
Dispersion of air pollution is a dynamic system. It non-
linearly depends on meteorological and other environ-
mental variables and not just on their present time values,
but also the variable’s history. Therefore the surrogate
models have to be dynamic models as well. A static model
would be just an approximation of a dynamic one in one
time instant. The purpose of the entire system of models is
forecasting for extended time horizons, therefore long-
range forecasting and the entire system of models has a
large number of outputs. The scheme of GIM is shown in
Fig. 4.
Dynamics is incorporated in a model with regressors,
which are the delayed values of outputs and inputs in the
form of inﬁnite-impulse-response or ﬁnite-impulse-re-
sponse models (Nelles 2002).
We selected a ﬁnite-impulse-response (FIR) model
structure for our submodels because an excessive number
of outputs would make their feedback very inconvenient.
These models have delayed values of inputs only (no
delayed outputs) for regressors and the number of delays
corresponds to the time in which impulse-excited response
fades out. Since air pollution dispersion is a nonlinear
process, we used a nonlinear-FIR (NFIR) model, in par-
ticular an ensemble model of bagged regression trees.
Regression trees were selected due to the speed of training
and their accuracy was improved using ensembles. Other
data-driven modelling methods were tested, but all have
performed worse than the selected one regarding the speed
of training.
The next step in the structure selection is the selection of
regressors. All seven available input signals were used as
inputs, while outputs were values of SO 2 at each cell. The
number of input delays was selected with 4-fold cross-
validation on the dataset of about 21,000 data points. The
reason for not taking a larger amount of data is that we
wanted to keep a reasonable computational time. The
training and validation sets were large enough to make the
obtained results instrumental also for larger datasets even
though the values of cost functions for cross-validation are
worse than in the case when a larger dataset is used.
The results of 4-fold cross-validation for delay-selection
are given in ‘ ‘ Appendix A ’ ’. Note that we have validated
the same amount of delays on all inputs, without elimi-
nating particular uninformative regressors due to simplic-
ity. Therefore, if the maximal delay is, e.g. 3, this means
that we have 21 regressors, 7 with delay 1, 7 with delay 2,
and 7 with delay 3 for the prediction of the value at the
moment of delay 0, i.e. at present moment. The cross-
validation study was pursued for the delay interval between
2 and 6, where the minimum was located.
The best SMSE and FMS results were obtained with the
delay of 4 samples, which corresponds to delays up to 2 h.
This can be interpreted that a transient of 2 h encompasses
the most information about the pollution dispersion.
The number of observations per tree leaf (or partition)
was selected next. Using the already selected model
parameters, a 4-fold cross-validation study was done to
determine the optimal number of observations. The
obtained results are given in ‘ ‘ Appendix A ’ ’. Averages of
the SMSE measure are shown in Fig. 5. SMSE was used
for the evaluation because we are evaluating the prediction
ability of each independent submodel in the GIM model.
It is clear from Fig. 5 that the prediction-quality index is
the lowest when 10 observations per tree leaf are used.
The next selection concerns the structure of ensembles,
in particular the number of regression models within the
ensemble. Using the already selected model parameters, a
4-fold cross-validation study was done to determine the

4.2 Reduced grid with interpolation
of outputs—RGI
RGI is intended as the structure for the acceleration of
computation in the comparison with GIM. The same data
was used for modelling and testing and with the same
division as in the case of GIM.
4.2.1 Structure
The entire model is composed of two parts: GIM, but not
for the complete grid, and the Gaussian-process grid for
ﬁlling up the gaps in the grid of predictions. The scheme of
RGI is shown in Fig. 11.
The structure of independent cell models was kept as it
was for the complete GIM. We selected every third cell to
be modelled, which reduced the number of cells to be
modelled on 34 /C2 34 ¼ 1156 cells. This is a considerable
reduction. In our case, the cells to be modelled with
independent models are distributed uniformly, but this is
not necessary.
Predictions of available independent cell models were
inputs into the GP grid. The GP grid uses covariance
functions for the calculation of the grid-based covariance
matrix. The individual covariance functions in our case
were two squared exponential covariance functions with
isotropic distance measures, each of them as
Cðxi; xjÞ¼ r2f exp /C0 r22l2/C18/C19 : ð8Þ
The hyperparameter r2f represents the scaling factor of the
possible variations of the function or the vertical scaling
factor and the hyperparameter l is called the horizontal
scaling factor and determines the relative weight on dis-
tance for the input variable x. The variable r is the input-
distance measure and is r ¼j xi /C0 xj j, where x is a
regression vector for the GP grid. In RGI’s case, regressors
of the GP grid are the cell’s indices.
The Kronecker covariance matrix (Wilson and Nickisch
2015) is calculated from two covariance matrices, each for
one input dimension.
Hyperparameters r2f and l were optimised for the best
grid performance.

The acceptable accuracy of a surrogate model depends
on the purpose of the model. The modeller has to put

The objective of our investigation was to develop a sur-
rogate model that will replace the air pollution Lagrangian
particle dispersion model for computationally intensive
applications like computer experimentations at a consid-
erably lower computational time. We proposed two meth-
ods, i.e. GIM and RGI, that considerably raise the potential

The computational load for surrogate model development

Other studies using surrogate models have not tackled

title: Application of DNM And Hec-Ras Model For Pollutant Dispersion Patterns in Rivers
abstract: In recent years, rapid urbanization has significantly impacted water quality in urban areas. Accurate prediction models for pollutant dispersion play a pivotal role in enhancing our ability to respond effectively to pollution incidents and promote sustainable urban development. However, the computational cost brought by traditional simulation models is relatively high and time-consuming. To address this problem, surrogate models are employed to enable efficient and rapid evaluations. This paper proposes a simulation-based prediction method for river water quality. First, a one-dimensional hydrodynamic water quality model is established by HEC-RAS. The riverbed data is derived through cubic spline difference, facilitating the simulation of the water pollutant transport process. Secondly, the hydraulic and water quality simulation results are obtained from the model constructed above. Subsequently, the simulation results are used as input to a deep neural network for further training and learning processes. By evaluating the applicability of deep learning models in predicting water pollution, this method can provide a valuable reference for urban water governance.

Abstract 
In recent years, rapid urbanization has significantly impacted water quality in urban areas. A ccurate 
prediction models for pollutant dispersion play a pivotal role in enhancing our ability to respond 
effectively to pollution incidents and promote sustainable urban development. However, the 
computational cost brought by traditional simulation models is relatively high and time -consuming. To 
address this problem, surrogate models are employed to enable efficient and rapid evaluations. This 
paper proposes a simulation -based prediction method for ri ver water quality. First, a one -dimensional 
hydrodynamic water quality model is established by HEC -RAS. The riverbed data is derived through 
cubic spline difference, facilitating the simulation of the water pollutant transport process. Secondly, the 
hydraulic and water quality simulation results are obtained from the model constructed above. 
Subsequently, the simulation results are used as input to a deep neural network for further training and 
learning processes. By evaluating the applicability of deep learning models in predicting water pollution, 
this method can provide a valuable reference for urban water governance.

Keywords: water quality, deep neural network, HEC-RAS model, pollutant dispersion. 
1. Introduction 
The rapid pace of modernization has give n rise to a multitude of environmental challenges, with water 
resource pollution being a prominent concern. To enhance the ability to address pollution incidents 
effectively, it is imperative to investigate the pollutant dispersion patterns in urban rivers to effectively 
predict key water quality indicators. Pollutant dispersion simulation methods mainly include data-driven 
modeling methods and physic -based methods according to dispersion mechanisms, such as using 
cellular automata to simulate the dispersion process of water pollutants or establishing an instantaneous 
point source pollution model to dynamically simulate the ch anges in river pollutant concentration over 
time[1]. In contrast to data-driven models, widely employed simulation software such as MIKE21, QUAL-
II, and WASP offer rapid and precise simulations of the pollut ant migration process[2]. The Hydrologic 
Engineering Center's River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) model, originally developed for the U.S. Army 
Corps of Engineers, is capable of performing steady -state and unsteady -state one-dimensional water 
quality simulation and two -dimensional hydrodynamic calculations [3]. Consequently, this study adopts 
the HEC-RAS framework for conducting simulation-based research on the pollutant dispersion process 
in urban rivers. 
Physic-based simulations of pollutant dispersion in urban rivers necessitate a substantial quantity of 
boundary parameters derived from practical scenarios, which generally results in significant 
computational costs. In recent years, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising approach to serve 
as a surrogate model to address complex environmental challenges [4], [5]. In this study, we apply DL 
techniques to conduct hydrodynamic modeling and water quality assessment. HEC -RAS is first

[с. 2]
employed to construct a physic-based hydrodynamic and pollutant dispersion model. Subsequently, the 
data obtained from the HEC-RAS model is input into a deep neural network (DNN) for training. As a 
surrogate model, DNN is able to predict pollutant concentrations at different profiles and reduce the 
required calculation time while maintaining a better accuracy performance. 
2. Methodology

dimensional steady flow simulation and one -dimensional unsteady flow simulation. The water surface 
line calculation of steady flow is based on the one-dimensional energy equation as depicted in Eq(1).

2.2. Pollutant dispersion model 
The water quality analysis module can simulate the migration of multiple water quality factors such as 
algae, water temperature (WT), dissolved oxygen (DO), particulate organic carbon (POC), nitrate (NO3), 
and total phosphorus (TP). Before conducting pollutant dispersion simulation, a feasible hydrodynamic 
module must be built first, and the simulation period shall also be limited to the time range of the 
hydrodynamic simulation. The simulation process requires the collection of a co mplete meteorological 
data set including atmospheric pressure, air temperature, humidity, solar shortwave radiation, cloud 
thickness, wind speed, and other meteorological data. HEC-RAS formulates the basic equation of one-
dimensional pollutant migration and transformation in rivers based on the principle of mass conservation 
(Eq(5)).

2.3. Deep Neural Network Models 
The construction of multiple hidden layers and the training data are the keys to improve the performance 
of the DNN model (Figure 1). DNN has nonlinear mapping capabilities and is commonly used to analyze 
complex nonlinear problems [6]. Three types of layers (i.e., input layer, output layer, and hidden layer) 
are contained in a DNN structure . These layers are fully interconnected, and information propagation 
between them adheres to the formula y = ωx + b and an activation function. Each connection has a 
unique weight (ω) and bias (b). Activation functions play a pivotal role in capturing nonlinear 
relationships among variables. Commonly used activation functions include the Sigmoid and Relu 
functions. This study applies DNN networks to the river pollutant dispersion simulation to achieve rapid 
prediction of water quality. 
 
Fig. 1. DNN structure diagram 
2.4. Boundary conditions 
The Xiantao segment of Hanjiang River was selected as the study area. The upper reaches of the river 
are 300 meters away from the Tianmen Bridge, while the lower reaches are in close proximity to Shiji 
Village. To establish a comprehensive understanding of the river’s topography, we utilized digital 
elevation model (DEM) data with a resolution of 12.5 m from publicly available datasets. Channel 
centerlines, shorelines, and basin lines are added based on the chann el outline. Additionally, we 
positioned profiles along the river at intervals ranging from 500 to 1000 meters. These profiles were 
essential for capturing the intricate terrain variations within the river channel. Notably, due to the 
challenging topography and the need to account for reduced spacing between profiles at bends and 
turns, a total of 80 profiles were obtained. The profile IDs span a range from 100 (minimum) to 67000 
(maximum), providing a comprehensive dataset for further analysis. The river profile is shown in Figure 
2. 
 
Fig.2. River topographic parameter map 
In the river topography modeling, the DEM data often lacks specific information regarding the riverbed 
topography. To address this limitation, the author employed the cubic spline interpolation method to

[с. 4]
derive the riverbed topographic data based on elevation data collected from both sides of the river [7]. 
Additionally, the constructed river channel model underwent calibration using topographic maps sourced 
from Google Earth . The resulting river channel profile, obtained through cubic spline interpolation, is 
visually represented in Figure 3. This approach enables a more accurate representation of the riverbed 
topography, enhancing the overall fidelity of the modeling process.

Where 𝐻 is the average water depth; 𝑢 is the average flow velocity of the profile; 𝐵 is the average 
water surface width of the river profile; 𝑗 is the hydraulic gradient; 𝑢∗ is the friction coefficient. 
3.Results and discussion 
In this section, the authors conduct hydrodynamic simulation using HEC -RAS, and the simulated data 
is then imported into a DNN for training and validation. 
3.1. Simulation results of hydrodynamic model 
The simulation time interval is defined from November 30, 2021, to December 15, 2021, with a 
simulation time step of one day. The upstream inflow profile is identified by profile ID 67000, while the 
downstream outflow profile corresponds to profile ID 100. Profile ID 11291 downstream is selected for 
model validation. The upstream boundary condition is specified using the water level, and the 
downstream boundary condition is set to normal depth. The initial conditions were set at a still water 
start. As depic ted in Figure 4, the hydrodynamic simulation exhibits a maximum error of 1.60% on 
December 13th, with the exception of the second day, which incurred an error of 7.15% . The high 
accuracy of the hydrodynamic simulation has established a foundation for subsequent water quality 
simulations.

[с. 5]
Fig.4. comparison of simulation results of profile ID 11291 
3.2. Simulation results of pollutant dispersion model 
Pollutant dispersion simulation is conducted based on higher hydrodynamic simulation accuracy. The 
main water quality factors in the Xiantao segment of the Hanjiang River include permanganate, ammonia 
nitrogen (NH 3-N), total phosphorus (TP), and dissolved oxygen (DO). Leveraging available data, we 
specifically focus on permanganate and TP for detailed simulation analysis and the missing data were 
completed using linear interpolation. At the same time, due to the mismatch between the actual water 
quality and the hydrodynamic measurement time, a reduction facto r is applied to rectify the pollutant 
simulation process. The modeling framework integrates critical parameters, including water quality data, 
meteorological datasets, dispersion coefficients, and initial conditions. These inputs are incorporated 
into the NSMI module within the HEC-RAS software, facilitating the construction of an initial water quality 
model. The simulation time step is set at 15 minutes to capture dynamic variations . The simulation 
results are shown in Figure 5. The maximum error has been reduced to 6.35% as shown in Table 1.

3.3. Analysis of DNN prediction results 
To obtain the training data for the DNN model, the HEC -RAS model was used to simulate different 
pollutant concentrations occurring in the upper reaches of the river profile, thereby obtaining 
concentration data of water quality indicators in the downstream profile. The DNN model was 
implemented using the Python programming language. Its input parameters consist of permanganate 
concentrations from different upstream profil es during a pollution event. The desired output is the 
permanganate concentration corresponding to downstream profile ID 45116. To optimize the model's 
performance, a K -fold cross -validation approach was employed to determine the optimal number of 
hidden layers. As was shown in Figure 6, the highest average R2 value of 0.983 was obtained with a 
configuration of two hidden layers, each comprising six neurons. Simultaneously, the root mean square 
error (RMSE) was 0.117, indicating a relatively low level of predictive error . In general, the DNN model 
demonstrates high prediction accuracy in predicting water quality in the specified region. 
 
Fig.6. Performance of (a) R2 and (b) RMSE under different hidden layers and neurons 
4. Conclusion 
In this research, the HEC -RAS software is employed to establish hydrodynamic and water quality 
models for the Xiantao profile of the Hanjiang River. Specifically, we conduct one-dimensional unsteady 
flow simulations and pollutant dispersion process simulations, focusing on the dispersion process of 
permanganate and TP. The maximum error in pollutant dispersion simulation is 6.35%, indicating a high 
level of prediction accuracy. To overcome the challenge of the high computing cost of physic -based 
models, we integrate the HEC-RAS model with DNN. The DNN is trained using data obtained from the 
HEC-RAS simulations, and K-fold cross-validation is performed to assess model performance. The DNN 
exhibited optimal R 2 performance of 0.98 under the parameter setting of two hidden layers and six 
neurons, which verifies the satisfactory prediction accuracy of the model. Consequently, the DNN model 
can serve as a surrogate model for the physic-based model to predict water pollutant concentrations in 
the specified region, thereby providing valuable insights for local water quality management.

title: High-fidelity CFD modelling of urban pollutant dispersion for air quality assessment
abstract: La vegetació en zones urbanes constitueix una estratègia primordial per mitigar els efectes de l'illa de calor urbana (UHI), però la seva influència en la ventilació i la dispersió de contaminants continua sent un fenomen complex. Mentre que la Dinàmica de Fluids Computacional (CFD) proporciona la fidelitat necessària per analitzar aquestes interaccions, el seu alt cost computacional limita el seu ús a gran escala. Els models substituts emergents ofereixen una solució eficient, però la seva precisió depèn completament de la qualitat del conjunt de dades amb els quals s'entrenen. Per a fer front a aquest repte, aquesta tesi desenvolupa un marc complet de CFD dissenyat per a servir com a generador de dades per a emuladors d'aprenentatge autònom. S'ha partit de la configuració clàssica de canó urbà i s'ha ampliat per incorporar un model físic robust de vegetació, tractant-la com un medi porós. Aquest plantejament vincula la resistència aerodinàmica i la generació de turbulència amb els intercanvis d'energia associats al refredament per evapotranspiració i a les ombres generades tant per les estructures com per les mateixes plantes. Per mitjà d'un estudi paramètric, s'han estudiat els efectes de la regulació tèrmica i la qualitat de l'aire. Les simulacions revelen que mentre que les configuracions amb arbres densos aconsegueixen baixar les temperatures a peu de carrer, també obstrueixen el flux d'aire, reduint significativament la ventilació. A més, s'ha observat que l'escalfament de les façanes i la mateixa vegetació generen vòrtexs secundaris que alteren els patrons de dispersió. Aquest treball aporta un model de simulació capaç de produir els conjunts de dades fonamentals per a potenciar els models d'intel·ligència artificial actuals.

Abstract
Urban greenery constitutes a primary strategy for mitigating the Urban Heat Island (UHI)
eﬀect, yet its inﬂuence on ventilation and pollutant dispersion remains a complex phe-
nomenon. While Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) provides the necessary ﬁdelity
to analyse these interactions, its high computational cost limits its use in large-scale ur-
ban design. Emerging data-driven surrogate models oﬀer an eﬃcient solution, but their
accuracy depends completely on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
To address this challenge, this thesis develops a comprehensive CFD framework designed
to serve as a data generator for machine-learning emulators. The canonical street-canyon
conﬁguration is extended to incorporate a robust physical model of vegetation by treating
it as a porous medium. This formulation couples aerodynamic drag and turbulence pro-
duction with energy exchanges associated with evapotranspirative cooling and dynamic
shading from the surrounding structures and vegetation.
A parametric study is conducted to quantify the trade-oﬀs between thermal regulation and
air quality. The simulations reveal that while conﬁgurations with dense foliage succeed in
lowering street-level temperatures, they also obstruct airﬂow, leading to a trapping eﬀect
that signiﬁcantly reduces ventilation. Furthermore, secondary buoyancy-driven vortices
generated by wall heating and vegetation fundamentally alter dispersion patterns. This
work presents a CFD model capable of producing the foundational dataset necessary to
extend the input space of existing AI surrogates to enable holistic urban microclimate
prediction.

1 Introduction
Air quality in urban areas is a growing concern due to its impact on public health and the
environment, with street canyons being especially vulnerable to pollutant accumulation.
The characteristic vortices generated within them obstruct eﬀective ventilation and trap
contaminants at street level. These ventilation ineﬃciencies are especially severe in the
worst-case ventilation conﬁguration, which consists of a square street canyon subjected
to wind perpendicular to the street axis, strengthening recirculation and signiﬁcantly
reducing air exchange. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is a key tool for analysing
these complex environments, but its high computational cost limits large-scale studies.
Data-driven models oﬀer an eﬃcient alternative by emulating the complex physics of
ﬂow, heat transfer and pollutant dispersion; however, existing models often omit the
critical impact of vegetation. The objective of this thesis is to bridge this gap by applying
established vegetation parameterisations within the CFD model, thereby generating the
necessary data to enhance these surrogate models for more realistic urban planning.
1.1 Motivation
Improving air quality in urban environments has become an urgent necessity, as the World
Health Organization (WHO) identiﬁes it as the greatest environmental threat to public
well-being. With global urban populations projected to reach 68% by 2050 [1], major
cities around the world are already facing critical levels of pollution, leading to signiﬁcant
impacts on public health. The continuous growth in urban density and traﬃc worsens
this issue, making the ability to assess, predict and mitigate pollution an essential tool for
sustainable urban planning.
To analyse these complex urban environments, CFD simulations are a widely established
scientiﬁc tool, but their elevated computational cost limits their practical application.
Data-driven models oﬀer an eﬃcient alternative to this challenge, emulating CFD results
at a signiﬁcantly lower cost. However, the predictive power of these models is entirely
dependent on the quality of their training data. A signiﬁcant gap in most of the current
approaches, including those recently developed, is the omission of urban vegetation. As
trees constantly alter ﬂow conditions, their absence in the training datasets creates a blind
spot in the resulting predictions. Addressing this gap is essential for the development of
truly holistic models.
1

[с. 12]
High-Fidelity CFD Modelling of Urban
Pollutant Dispersion for Air Quality Assessment
1.2 State of the Art
To accurately model the inﬂuence of vegetation on urban environments, CFD simulations
typically incorporate speciﬁc parameterisations. Vegetation is commonly represented as
a porous medium that interacts with the surrounding airﬂow, requiring the inclusion of
additional terms in the governing equations of ﬂuid dynamics.
The primary aerodynamic eﬀect of vegetation is the reduction in wind speed caused by
drag from foliage. This is modelled by adding a sink term to the momentum equation.
The foundational formulations describing the eﬀects of vegetation on both mean ﬂow and
turbulence through these additional terms were ﬁrst presented in seminal works by Green
[2], Liu et al. [3] and Sanz [4].
Building on this framework, Buccolieri et al. [5] provided a key advancement for practical
applications in urban areas. Through a combination of wind tunnel experiments and
numerical simulations, they introduced a methodology to empirically determine the drag
eﬀects of the canopy. They characterised the vegetation’s resistance to airﬂow using a
pressure loss coeﬃcient, an inertial loss term based on direct measurements of porous
materials in a wind tunnel. This approach provided a robust method for parameterising
the momentum sink of trees in CFD simulations.
Beyond simply reducing wind speed, vegetation also alters the turbulence levels of the
ﬂow. The wakes generated by leaves and branches enhance turbulence, which must be
accounted for in turbulence modelling. This is handled by adding source terms to the
governing equations for the turbulent quantities.
As detailed by Amorim et al. [6], standard ﬂow equations were extended to incorporate the
aerodynamic eﬀects of trees on the wind ﬁeld. Their work focused on assessing how this
modiﬁed wind ﬂow aﬀects the dispersion of carbon monoxide from road traﬃc. By adding
these turbulence source terms, their model signiﬁcantly improved accuracy in predicting
pollutant concentrations at the pedestrian level compared to simulations that neglected
vegetation eﬀects.
More recently, Shen et al. [7] also applied this approach to investigate how diﬀerent
vegetation planting patterns aﬀect pollutant distribution within a street canyon. Their
numerical study conﬁrmed that these source terms are essential for capturing the complex
changes in airﬂow and pollutant dispersion caused by the presence of trees and greenbelts.

Pollutant Dispersion for Air Quality Assessment
Vegetation also plays a crucial role in regulating the urban thermal environment, primarily
by providing shade that reduces solar heating of surfaces. Furthermore, the cooling eﬀect
of evapotranspiration is represented by introducing a sink term in the energy equation.
Authors like Gromke et al. [8] and Moradpour et al. [9] introduced a constant volumetric
cooling term to model the transpirational heat removal in vegetated regions. While this
simpliﬁed method is eﬀective in certain scenarios, other physically-based models are also
commonly used. For instance, the parameterisation developed by Bruse et al. [10] and
applied by authors such as Yang et al. [11] and Defraeye et al. [12] models the thermal
eﬀect as a heat ﬂux term dynamically linked to local conditions. It deﬁnes heat transfer
as a function of leaf area density ( LAD), local wind speed and the temperature diﬀerence
between foliage and ambient air, providing more accurate solutions of the plant-atmosphere
energy exchange.
This body of work is comprehensively reviewed by Buccolieri et al. [13], who summarise
the state-of-the-art parameterisations used in CFD to model the aerodynamic, deposition
and thermal eﬀects of urban vegetation. Their review conﬁrms that this framework is
the most eﬀective method for integrating the complex inﬂuence of vegetation into urban
environmental simulations.
1.3 Objectives
The principal objective of this thesis is to develop a high-ﬁdelity CFD model capable of
simulating the microclimate within an urban street canyon, with a speciﬁc focus on inte-
grating the eﬀects of vegetation. Three interconnected strands of work support this core
aim. First, the model will incorporate state-of-the-art parameterisations for vegetation,
treating it as a porous medium, alongside accurate energy boundary conditions to capture
solar loading and thermal exchange. Second, the predictive reliability of the developed
framework will be evaluated through validation against a benchmark case for vegetated
scenarios, which provides both wind tunnel measurements and reference CFD data for
comparison. Finally, the validated model will be employed in a targeted parametric study
to provide a preliminary quantiﬁcation of the inﬂuence of key variables on the resultant
ﬁelds. The outcome of this work is to provide the basis for generating a robust dataset,
designed to enhance the physical ﬁdelity of training data for machine learning-based sur-
rogate models of the urban environment.

2 Methodology
2.1 Physical Model
This thesis presents a comprehensive numerical investigation based on two-dimensional
stationary Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations. The primary objective
is to quantify the impact of urban vegetation on the microclimatic conditions and pollutant
dispersion within an idealised street canyon.
This work extends the methodology developed by Moreira et al. [14] by integrating a
comprehensive vegetation parameterisation, including all physical processes described later
in Section 2.2.3. Within the scope of this thesis, the focus is placed on developing the
foundation of a database by modelling vegetation eﬀects and reﬁning the energy boundary
conditions through a heat-ﬂux-based approach, assessing their inﬂuence on the ﬂow and
pollutant dispersion. This approach provides a basis for more accurate simulations of
urban microclimates and for future studies in street canyon environments.
The study is conducted in the computational domain illustrated in Figure 2.1. The geome-
try represents a canonical urban environment and is designed to ensure a robust numerical
solution independent of boundary eﬀects.

A pollutant line source is deﬁned at street level, centred on the canyon ﬂoor and located

2.3 Numerical Setup
The numerical model has been solved using the Finite Element Method (FEM) imple-
mented in COMSOL Multiphysics v6.3 [23], following the same setup described by Mor-
eira et al. [14]. The same discretisation order (P1+P1) and SUPG stabilisation with
streamline and crosswind diﬀusion have been applied.
Regarding the mesh, a mapped structured grid has been generated in the street-canyon
region due to the inclusion of vegetation elements. This area has been reﬁned using
square elements with a characteristic length of 0.1 m to better capture the local ﬂow
and scalar gradients. The rest of the computational domain has been meshed with a
coarser structured quadrilateral grid, ensuring smooth transitions between regions and
maintaining computational eﬃciency.
As noted in Section 2.1, the computational domain has been deﬁned using the same
methodology as in Moreira et al. [14], which complies with the recommended guidelines for
CFD modelling of urban ﬂows [24]. The ﬁnal grid contains 84,032 quadrilateral elements,
providing adequate resolution in the canyon region.

3 Results
3.1 Model Validation
Before directly addressing the research questions of this thesis, model validation is nec-
essary to ensure the reliability of the numerical setup. The objective of this validation
is to demonstrate that the model can accurately reproduce physical phenomena under
controlled conditions. This is achieved by comparing the simulation results with estab-
lished experimental data, verifying that the model can faithfully replicate complex airﬂow
patterns around vegetation.
For this purpose, the validation procedure is based on the methodology presented by Liang
et al. [25]. This involves numerically replicating their wind tunnel study of airﬂow through
a small forest stand. A key feature of this study is that, rather than treating LAD and
the drag coeﬃcient as constants, the model deﬁnes both as functions of height, allowing
for a more realistic diﬀerentiation between the aerodynamic behaviour of the tree trunks
and that of the upper canopy. Successfully reproducing the results of this experiment,
the chosen numerical schemes, turbulence models and vegetation parameterisations are
veriﬁed as appropriate for this ﬁeld of study.
The simulation was conducted using a two-dimensional domain, as shown in Figure 3.1.
In the original wind tunnel experiment, however, the domain had a depth of 25H , with the
vegetation centrally positioned along this depth and occupying a 5-metre-wide strip. This
distinction is important to note, as the dimensionality of the vegetation may inﬂuence the
ﬂow and should be considered when interpreting the results.

3.2 Convergence
3.2.1 Mesh Convergence
A mesh convergence analysis has been conducted monitoring the average concentration at
the leeward wall. Due to the complex source terms introduced to model vegetation and
heat transfer, coarse meshes failed to resolve local gradients, leading to solver divergence;
consequently, only reﬁned grids capable of sustaining physical solutions are presented. As
shown in Figure 3.3a, the solution stabilises after overcoming initial sensitivity. A grid of
84,032 elements has been selected, yielding a relative error of less than 0.4% compared to
the ﬁnest reference. This conﬁguration has been chosen to guarantee the stability of the
model while maintaining computational eﬃciency.
3.2.2 Domain Convergence
To ensure the independence of the results from the computational boundaries, a speciﬁc
convergence analysis has been performed. Since the upstream and downstream lengths
have been established as suﬃcient to resolve the ﬂow development and the wake regions,
the study has focused on the domain height. The objective has been to determine a
vertical clearance large enough to prevent artiﬁcial acceleration of the ﬂow due to the top
boundary. As illustrated in Figure 3.3b, diﬀerent domain heights have been evaluated,
studying the variation in ﬂow variables. A ﬁnal domain height of 8 H has been selected,
as it leads to a relative error of less than 0.5% compared to larger domains, ensuring that
the blockage eﬀect is negligible.

3.3 Velocity Field
Results of the parametric study for LAD ={0, 1, 2} m−1 and θ ={45◦, 90◦, 135◦} are

the main recirculation vortex core towards the upper-right section of the canyon, while
small secondary recirculation zones form beneath the tree crowns due to ﬂow separation.

The temperature ﬁeld distributions in Figure 3.5 show that vegetation signiﬁcantly reduces

driven by the ﬂow pattern: windward heating sweeps hot air into the main recirculation,
trapping heat throughout the canyon, whereas air heated by the leeward wall is quickly
released into the upper atmosphere, allowing for more eﬀective ventilation. Localised
heating is also observed on the exterior of the tree crowns due to direct solar radiation.

3.5 Pollutant Concentration
The pollutant concentration plots for the parametric study are presented in Figure 3.6.
The concentration ﬁeld reveals that the aerodynamic drag induced by the vegetation signif-
icantly decreases air exchange eﬃciency, leading to reduced ventilation. This is evidenced
by the non-vegetated scenarios ( LAD = 0 m−1), which maintain a much more uniform
and diluted dispersion, resulting in notably lower concentrations near the leeward wall
compared to the vegetated cases. In contrast, the concentration near the windward wall
is slightly higher in the non-vegetated cases than in the vegetated scenarios. Overall, the

4 Conclusions
This thesis has developed a comprehensive CFD framework to simulate the complex mi-
croclimatic interactions within an urban street canyon. A robust physical model treating
vegetation as a porous medium has been successfully implemented, integrating momen-
tum sinks for aerodynamic drag, turbulence sources for canopy-induced mixing and energy
terms for evapotranspirative cooling, as well as an accurate shading model. The numerical
setup has been validated against wind tunnel experimental data and other RANS models,
demonstrating strong agreement for mean velocity and TKE proﬁles.
The parametric study has revealed a critical trade-oﬀ in the ﬂow dynamics of the street
canyon. While high LAD conﬁgurations have been shown to signiﬁcantly mitigate heat
stress, they have simultaneously been observed to obstruct airﬂow, leading to a trapping
eﬀect where pollutant concentrations increase, particularly near the leeward wall. Further-
more, in speciﬁc thermal scenarios, wall heating has been identiﬁed to trigger a secondary
buoyant vortex. Although not included in the presented results, additional simulations
indicate that under certain parameter combinations this thermally induced recirculation
can strengthen considerably, potentially raising pollutant concentrations at pedestrian
level and on the windward side.
Ultimately, this work establishes a foundational framework for generating physically en-
riched datasets required to advance data-driven modelling in urban environments. By
extending the parametric space to include vegetation, this framework enables the future
training of machine-learning surrogate models.
4.1 Future Work
Future research should concentrate on developing a high-ﬁdelity CFD database that spans
the extended parameter space, providing the foundation for training surrogate models
aimed at accelerating urban microclimate predictions. Another promising direction in-
volves using these surrogates to systematically identify critical ﬂow regimes, particularly
those produced by speciﬁc combinations of wall heating and vegetation that give rise to
secondary buoyant vortices or canopy-induced ﬂow separation. In addition, a global sen-
sitivity analysis should be undertaken to quantify the relative inﬂuence of thermal and
vegetative parameters, thereby informing dimensionality reduction and the construction
of more eﬃcient predictive frameworks.
